items.prompt:
Which word is a TEMPORAL WORD that helps show the order of events in a narrative?
A) because
B) also
C) finally
D) since

steps: Temporal words show when or in what order events happen. 'Finally' signals the last event. 'Because,' 'also,' and 'since' are not temporal order words.

items.prompt:
What should a narrative ENDING do?
A) Introduce a new character
B) List all the events again
C) Give the story a sense of closure and show how the character feels
D) State the topic of the story for the first time

steps: A narrative ending wraps up the story. It should make the reader feel the story is complete, often by showing how the character feels or what they learned.

items.prompt:
Which sentence is the BEST beginning for a narrative?
A) Finally, I went to sleep.
B) One rainy afternoon, my sister and I decided to build a cardboard box city on the living room floor.
C) Then I found a big box.
D) I like rainy days.

steps: A good narrative beginning sets the scene. Option B tells WHO, WHEN, and WHERE, and introduces what the story will be about. A and C are middle/end sentences; D is too vague.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative sentence: 'I was scared.' Which revised sentence adds a feeling detail that SHOWS rather than TELLS the emotion?
A) 'I felt really scared.'
B) 'I was very scared indeed.'
C) 'My hands shook and my heart hammered as I stood at the top of the tall diving board.'
D) 'Scared is what I was.'

steps: 'Show, don't tell' means using actions and physical sensations to express emotions instead of simply naming them. Option C shows fear through shaking hands and a hammering heart.

items.prompt:
A student's narrative about a snowstorm uses the word 'said' four times. Which word is the BEST replacement for 'said' in: '"Watch out!" she said as the snowball flew toward my face.'?
A) whispered
B) mumbled
C) shrieked
D) sighed

steps: 'Watch out!' is an urgent warning. 'Shrieked' matches that urgency best. 'Whispered' and 'mumbled' suggest a quiet voice; 'sighed' expresses tiredness or sadness.

items.prompt:
Which of the following sequences is the CORRECT structure for a narrative?
A) Middle, ending, beginning
B) Beginning, ending, middle
C) Beginning, middle, ending
D) Ending, beginning, middle

steps: A narrative is structured as: beginning (who/when/where), middle (events in order using temporal words), ending (closure/feeling).

items.prompt:
Read this 4-sentence narrative. Identify the ONE sentence that is out of place and explain why.

'Last spring, my class planted a vegetable garden in the schoolyard. First, we dug small holes and dropped seeds into the soil. Vegetables are an important part of a healthy diet. Then we watered the garden every other day and watched tiny green sprouts appear over the next few weeks.'
items.answer: 'Vegetables are an important part of a healthy diet.' This sentence does not belong because it is a factual statement that belongs in informative writing, not a narrative. It does not describe an event, a feeling, or an action that is part of the story sequence.

steps: In a narrative, every sentence should move the story forward by describing events, actions, or feelings.
A general fact about vegetables breaks the story flow and belongs in a different type of writing.

items.prompt: Write a complete 4-sentence narrative about exploring a new place. Include a beginning that creates a sense of setting, two middle events with different temporal words, and an ending sentence that reflects on what the experience meant to you.
items.answer: Sample: The summer I turned seven, my family drove deep into a national park I had never visited, where the trees were so tall and thick that even the midday sun could only reach us in thin gold stripes. First, we hiked a trail that wound along a rushing creek, and I stopped every few minutes to watch the water tumble over smooth, mossy rocks. Then we found a clearing where a family of deer grazed calmly in the afternoon light, so close I could have counted the spots on the youngest fawn. By the time we reached the car, dirty and tired and happy, I understood why some places feel less like destinations and more like answers to questions you didn't know you had.

steps: Beginning: vivid setting that immerses the reader.
First event: specific action or discovery.
Ending: reflection on what the experience meant.
